The Mount Batur sunrise trek is a pre-dawn climb of an active volcano in the Kintamani highlands, timed to reach the top for sunrise. Travel guides put the climb at about two hours from the lakeside village of Toya Bungkah, and say a local guide is required. The mountain is about 1,700 meters high, it is cold at the top, and the day starts in the middle of the night.

What Mount Batur is

Mount Batur is an active volcano of about 1,700 meters, roughly 5,600 feet, standing inside a large caldera in the Kintamani area of northeast Bali. A crater lake, Lake Batur, lies beside it. The caldera rim at Penelokan is the main viewpoint, described by travel guides as best early in the day before cloud forms.

Where it is

Kintamani is in the highlands, about 27 miles from Ubud by road, about 45 from Seminyak and about 48 from the airport. Those distances explain the schedule: a traveler staying in the south has a long drive before the walking begins. From Ubud the drive is shorter by a wide margin.

An active volcano

Batur is an active volcano, and access depends on its status. We have no live source for volcanic alerts, so check the current situation with your guide or accommodation before you book, and again the day before. A trek that is closed for safety is closed.

What the night looks like

The Batur trek is a short night followed by a short climb. A sunrise at the summit means walking in the dark, and walking in the dark means being collected from your hotel well before dawn. We give no clock times, since they vary by season, starting point and operator; ask yours for the pickup time.

The pickup

The earlier part of the night is a drive. The further your base is from Kintamani, the earlier the car comes. A stay in Ubud, or in the Kintamani area itself the night before, shortens that drive and lengthens your sleep. Our advice is not to attempt it from the far south.

The climb

Travel guides describe the route from Toya Bungkah as taking about two hours to the summit, with more than half of it through forest. The upper part is on open volcanic ground. You walk by flashlight or headlamp, in a line with other groups. We rate no difficulty; it is a steady uphill walk at night on a mountain.

At the top

The summit is cold before sunrise. Travel guides describe Kintamani as much cooler than the coast and advise a sweater or jacket. Cloud decides the view, and no one can promise a clear morning. The descent is in daylight, and many treks end with a visit to the hot springs in Toya Bungkah.

The guide requirement

A guide is required for the Batur climb, according to travel guides, and guides belong to the local Association of Mount Batur Trekking Guides, which has its office in Toya Bungkah. The same guides warn that touts target visitors in the area, and suggest booking the climb in advance.

Booking

Most visitors book the trek as a package that includes transport, the guide and breakfast. We quote no prices. Ask what is included, how large the group is, and whether the guide is a member of the local association. A booking made through your accommodation gives you someone to hold to account.

What to ask the operator

These are our own suggestions.

  • What time is pickup, and how long is the drive from my hotel?
  • How many people are in the group?
  • Is a flashlight or headlamp provided?
  • What happens if the mountain is closed or the weather is bad?

What to bring

Packing for Batur is packing for a cold, dark, dusty walk. Our advice: closed shoes with grip, a warm layer and a windproof one, a headlamp if you own one, water, and a small snack. Leave valuables at the hotel. A light scarf or buff helps with dust on the way down.

Fitness and health

The trek asks for a moderate level of fitness and sure footing in the dark. Anyone with a heart or breathing condition, a knee problem or a fear of heights should think carefully. The State Department says an injured traveler in Indonesia will likely need to reach a major city for appropriate care, and a mountain is a long way from one.

Insurance

Check how your travel insurance treats trekking and volcano climbs. Some policies list hiking above a certain altitude or on active volcanoes among their exclusions. Ask before the trip, in writing.

When in the trip to do it

The Batur trek fits best in the middle of a trip. On the first days, jet lag from the United States makes a traveler wake early, which helps, and also leaves them short of sleep, which does not. The CDC advises allowing at least two days to adjust before anything important.

The day after

Our advice is to keep the rest of trek day free. You will be back at your hotel by late morning having been awake since the small hours. Booking a long drive, a transfer to a new base or an evening event for the same day makes for a hard day.

Season

The dry months, from about May to October, are the conventional choice for a sunrise climb, since the point is a clear view. Climate figures for south Bali do not describe the mountains, so we give no rainfall numbers for Kintamani. In the wet season, ask about recent conditions before committing.

If you would prefer not to climb

The view of Batur does not require the climb. The caldera rim at Penelokan looks across the crater lake to the volcano, and travel guides describe the view as spectacular early in the day. It is reached by road, about 27 miles from Ubud, and suits anyone who wants the scenery without the night walk.

The temple and the lake

Pura Ulun Danu Batur, on the caldera rim, is one of Bali's main water temples and part of the island's UNESCO-listed rice-terrace and water-temple landscape. A day in Kintamani that combines the viewpoint, the temple and lunch is a gentler alternative to the trek.

FAQ

How long does the Mount Batur sunrise trek take?

Travel guides put the climb at about two hours from Toya Bungkah. With the drive and the descent, it takes most of a night and a morning.

Do you need a guide for Mount Batur?

Yes, according to travel guides. Guides belong to the local Association of Mount Batur Trekking Guides.

Is it cold on Mount Batur?

Yes. Kintamani is much cooler than the coast, and a sweater or jacket is advised for the summit before sunrise.

How high is Mount Batur?

About 1,700 meters, roughly 5,600 feet.

Bali works well with children when the trip is planned around a calm base, short drives and a pool. Sanur and Nusa Dua are the areas travel guides describe as suited to families. The matters that need thought in advance are car seats, which you should not expect to find, the water, the sun, mosquitoes and animals, and a first aid kit packed at home.

Choosing a family base

A family base in Bali should be calm, close to the airport and easy to move around. Travel guides describe Sanur as a mature resort town that appeals mostly to families and older visitors, and Nusa Dua as an enclave of high-end resorts with very little traffic. Sanur is about 11 miles from the airport and Nusa Dua about 8.

Sanur

Sanur is a town with a beach, on the east-facing coast. Its appeal for families is that it is quiet and walkable, with restaurants and shops at a small scale. It is also about 14 miles from Ubud, which makes a day trip to the rice terraces and temples realistic.

Nusa Dua

Nusa Dua is built around large resorts. For a family that wants a kids' club, several pools and everything on site, it is the obvious choice. It is less a place to explore than a place to stay put, and meals are mostly taken in the resort.

Ubud with children

Ubud suits older children who will enjoy rice terraces, temples and the Monkey Forest. It has no beach, and the town center is congested. A pool matters more here than on the coast. Our advice is to give Ubud two or three nights in the middle of a longer stay by the sea.

Car seats and getting around

Car seats are the practical gap in a family trip to Bali. We have found no official source requiring child seats in cars there, and you should not expect a taxi, an app car or a driver's vehicle to carry one. If a seat matters to you, bring your own, or confirm one in writing with a driver before you travel.

Use a driver

A car with a driver booked for the day is the family way to get around. Ask in advance about seat belts in the back seats and about fitting a child seat. Keep drives short: plan one outing a day and count the drive back. We give no drive times, since they vary by hour.

Scooters

Families on scooters are a common sight in Bali and no model to follow. Indonesian law requires a helmet for every rider and passenger and a license matching the type of vehicle driven. Our advice is that children do not belong on a rented scooter.

Water, food and stomachs

Children are the travelers most likely to swallow tap water without thinking. The State Department says tap water in many areas of Indonesia is not safe to drink and advises sealed bottled water. The CDC's advice is to brush teeth with bottled water and to avoid ice where water safety is in doubt.

Habits to set on day one

Put a bottle of water by every sink. Teach children to keep their mouths closed in the shower and the pool. The CDC's food advice is to choose food that is cooked and served hot and to wash hands often with soap and water, especially before eating.

If a child gets sick

The CDC's advice for travelers' diarrhea is to drink plenty of fluids and to use oral rehydration solution in serious cases. Pack rehydration salts suitable for children. Dehydration develops faster in a small body, so our advice is to see a doctor early with a child and not to wait it out.

Sun, mosquitoes and animals

The three outdoor risks for children in Bali are sun, mosquitoes and animals. The CDC's advice on sun is to use sunscreen with an SPF of at least 15, wear protective clothing, and seek shade in the hottest part of the day, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Mosquitoes

The CDC says mosquitoes in Indonesia spread diseases, including dengue, that cannot be prevented with a vaccine or medicine, and that the mosquitoes concerned bite by day as well as at night. Its advice is to cover skin, use an appropriate repellent as directed on the label, and sleep in air-conditioned or screened rooms.

Animals

The CDC says dogs infected with rabies are commonly found in Indonesia and advises travelers to keep away from animals. Children are drawn to dogs, cats and monkeys. Set the rule before the trip: no touching any animal. Any bite or scratch needs washing and a doctor the same day.

Health preparation

A family trip to Bali starts at the pediatrician. The CDC recommends that travelers be current on routine vaccines and recommends hepatitis A, hepatitis B and typhoid for Indonesia. Ask about each child's schedule well before departure, since some vaccines need time.

Medicine

Bring children's medicines from home. The State Department warns that counterfeit medication is common in Indonesia. Prescription medicine should travel in its original packaging with the prescription, and over-the-counter medicine has its own small allowance at customs.

Insurance and care

The State Department highly recommends travel insurance for Indonesia and says hospitals often require payment or a deposit upfront. Check that the policy covers every member of the family, and save the assistance number. Ask your hotel on arrival which clinic it would send a child to.

Pools and the sea

A pool is the center of a family stay in Bali. Ask before booking whether a villa pool is fenced, since many are not. At the beach, we have no official source on sea conditions or lifeguards at any beach and call none safe. Ask the hotel where children can swim, and stay within reach.

The flight and the first days

The journey from the United States is long, with at least one connection, and the time difference is 12 hours or more. Children adjust on their own schedule. Keep the first two days empty, expect early mornings, and use them at the pool.

FAQ

Is Bali good for families with kids?

Yes, with a calm base and short drives. Travel guides describe Sanur and Nusa Dua as the areas suited to families.

Are car seats available in Bali?

Do not expect one in a taxi or a driver's car. Bring your own or confirm one in writing before you travel.

Can kids drink the water in Bali?

No. The State Department says tap water in many areas of Indonesia is not safe to drink. Use sealed bottled water, including for brushing teeth.

What vaccines do children need for Bali?

The CDC recommends being current on routine vaccines and recommends hepatitis A, hepatitis B and typhoid. Ask your pediatrician well ahead.

Ten days in Bali gives room for a third stop, and for most travelers the best use of it is a few nights on the Nusa islands. A workable shape is three nights in Ubud, three on Nusa Lembongan or Nusa Penida, and four at a beach base in the south. The island leg belongs in the middle, with the boat well clear of the flight home.

What ten days adds

Ten nights are three more than a week, and those three nights are what make a third base possible. A week covers Ubud and one coast base. Ten days add one more region without rushing the first two. The Nusa islands, off the southeast coast, are the closest addition, since boats leave from Sanur.

Why the islands

The three Nusa islands offer what the mainland's south does not: small-island days with very little traffic, cliffs, snorkeling and surf. Nusa Lembongan is about 8 square kilometers and nearly free of cars. Nusa Penida is far larger and wilder. Tiny Nusa Ceningan is joined to Lembongan by a bridge.

A ten-day route

The ten-day route below adds an island leg to the classic pairing of Ubud and the coast. It is a suggestion to adapt, with no prices and no drive times. It assumes ten nights and puts the boat crossings on days four and seven, away from both flights.

  • Days 1 to 3: Ubud.
  • Day 4: drive to Sanur, boat to Nusa Lembongan.
  • Days 5 and 6: Lembongan, Ceningan and a day on Nusa Penida.
  • Day 7: boat back to Sanur, transfer to a southern beach base.
  • Days 8 to 10: the coast.
  • Day 11: depart.

Days 1 to 3: Ubud

Ubud comes first, while jet lag wakes you early. It is about 22 miles from the airport. Walk the center on the first full day and take a driver to the rice terraces and temples on the second. Ubud is also about 13 miles from Sanur's harbor, which makes it a convenient place to leave from.

Days 4 to 6: the islands

Boats to the Nusa islands leave mainly from Sanur. Travel guides give the crossing as roughly 30 to 45 minutes and note that most boats to Lembongan involve a wet landing, wading from the beach. Stay on Lembongan and visit Penida from there; guides put that hop at about ten minutes by local boat.

Days 7 to 10: the coast

Return to Bali with three or four nights left, and spend them at a beach base that suits you: Seminyak, Canggu, the Bukit or Sanur itself. Sanur has the advantage of needing no transfer after the boat. These last days carry no boats and no long drives.

Why the boat goes in the middle

The island leg sits in the middle of this route for one reason. Boat crossings depend on sea conditions, and we have no official source on how often they are delayed or cancelled. A boat on day seven leaves several days of slack before the flight. A boat on day ten leaves none.

What travel guides say about boats

Travel guides advise against boarding any fast boat you have doubts about, whether because of the vessel, overloading or the weather. Take a morning boat, in daylight. Keep phones and passports in a dry bag, and carry luggage you can lift, since a wet landing means wading with it.

Lembongan or Penida for the nights

The two main islands suit different travelers. Lembongan is small, easy and built for visitors, with a choice of places to stay. Penida is about 247 square kilometers, with rough roads and simpler services. Our view is that Lembongan is the better base for a first island stay.

What to do there

Two full days on the islands cover a snorkeling trip, the cliffs of Lembongan's south coast, the bridge to Ceningan, and a day on one side of Penida. Travel guides warn of rip currents at Dream Beach and of fatal falls at Devil's Tear; stay behind the barriers.

Alternatives to the island leg

The islands are one way to use three extra nights, and not the only one. A traveler uneasy on boats can add East Bali instead: Sidemen is about 22 miles from Ubud, and Amed about 49. A traveler who wants mountains can add Munduk, about 39 miles from Ubud.

Choosing among them

These are our own suggestions. Choose the islands for sea, snorkeling and beaches. Choose Sidemen for rice terraces and walking without crowds. Choose Amed for diving from the shore. Choose Munduk for waterfalls and cool air. Each replaces the island leg in the middle of the route.

Practical points

A ten-night stay is well inside the 30 days the tourist visa allows. The visa costs IDR 500,000 and Bali's tourist levy is IDR 150,000 per person. Bring cash to the islands and any medicine you rely on, since both are harder to come by there.

Insurance

The State Department strongly recommends insurance that covers medical evacuation in Indonesia, and says an injured traveler will likely need to reach a major city for care. From an island, that begins with a boat. Check how your policy treats boat travel, snorkeling and motorbikes.

Where the slack goes

Ten days leave room for one spare day, and where you put it matters more than whether you have it. How the island leg, the spare day and the departure are spaced is set out in the complete Bali trip guide.

FAQ

Is 10 days enough for Bali?

Yes. Ten nights cover Ubud, a beach base and one more region, such as the Nusa islands.

How should I split 10 days in Bali?

Our suggestion is three nights in Ubud, three on the Nusa islands and four at a southern beach base.

Should I stay on Nusa Lembongan or Nusa Penida?

Our view is Lembongan for a first island stay, with a day visit to Penida, which is about ten minutes away by local boat.

When in the trip should I do the islands?

In the middle. Boats depend on the sea, so keep several days between the return crossing and your flight home.

Nusa Penida is better with a night than as a day trip, if your schedule allows it. The island is large, its roads are rough and its famous viewpoints are far apart, so a day trip from Bali covers one side of it in a hurry. An overnight stay gives you the cliffs early and late, without the day-trip crowd. A day trip still makes sense when time is short.

What Nusa Penida is

Nusa Penida is the largest of the three islands off Bali's southeast coast, at about 247 square kilometers, roughly 95 square miles. That is some thirty times the size of neighboring Nusa Lembongan. It is known for dramatic coastal cliffs and beaches, including Kelingking, Angel's Billabong, Broken Beach, Crystal Bay, Atuh Beach and Diamond Beach.

Why its size matters

Travel guides describe the roads on Nusa Penida as rough, and hilly away from the north coast. The best-known sights are split between the west side and the east side of the island. Reaching both in one day means spending most of it in a car on poor roads.

Getting there

Boats leave mainly from Sanur, with a slower ferry from Padang Bai. Travel guides give the speedboat crossing from Sanur as roughly 30 minutes, arriving at harbors on the north coast such as Toyapakeh, Buyuk and Sampalan. We have no official schedule; check times with the operator.

The case for a day trip

A day trip to Nusa Penida is the choice most visitors make, and it works for seeing one side of the island. Travel guides note that most visitors arrive on day trips from Bali. You leave Sanur in the morning, tour by car, and return in the afternoon, with no need to move your luggage.

What a day covers

A day realistically covers one side: the west, with Kelingking, Angel's Billabong, Broken Beach and Crystal Bay, or the east, with Atuh and Diamond Beach. We give no drive times, since we have no source for them. Our advice is to pick a side and not to let a tour promise both.

The drawbacks

Day trips share the same hours on the island, so our expectation is that the viewpoints are busiest in the middle of the day. The day also depends on two boat crossings fitting around it, and a late morning boat leaves less time for sightseeing.

The case for staying overnight

Staying overnight on Nusa Penida changes what the visit is. Accommodation exists along the north coast between Toyapakeh and Sampalan. With a night or two, you can reach a viewpoint early in the morning or late in the afternoon, and you can see both sides of the island on separate days.

What two days allow

Two days allow one side each, with time to walk down to a beach instead of only looking at it from above. They also leave room for a snorkeling trip; Manta Point, off the island's coast, is a known site for manta rays. We promise no sightings.

What it costs you

An overnight means carrying your luggage across on the boat and accepting simpler services than on Bali. Travel guides describe the roads as rough. The State Department says an injured traveler in Indonesia will likely need to reach a major city, which from Penida begins with a boat.

Safety on the island

Nusa Penida's scenery comes with real hazards, and travel guides say so. They describe the path down to Kelingking Beach as a clifftop descent of about 400 meters, and Peguyangan Spring as reached by about 700 stairs on a cliff edge. They also warn of heat, and against swimming at Broken Beach at high tide because of the waves.

The beaches below the cliffs

The beaches under the viewpoints are open to ocean swell. We have no official source on currents at any of them and call none safe for swimming. Our advice is to admire most of them from the sand, and to ask local people before entering the water anywhere.

Motorbikes

Travel guides describe Penida's roads as rough and hilly. Indonesia's traffic law requires a license matching the type of vehicle driven. Our advice is to hire a car with a local driver.

Insurance

The State Department strongly recommends insurance that covers medical evacuation in Indonesia. Check before the trip how your policy treats motorbike riding and boat travel, and keep the insurer's assistance number in your phone.

How to choose

The choice between a day trip and an overnight on Nusa Penida depends on how many days you have and what you want from the island. Choose a day trip if your whole stay is a week and you want a look at the famous cliffs. Choose an overnight if you have ten days or more, or care about photographs without crowds.

A middle way

A third option is to stay on Nusa Lembongan and visit Penida from there. Travel guides give the crossing between the two islands as about ten minutes by local boat. That gives you Lembongan's easier accommodation with Penida as a short hop.

Book the boat with daylight to spare

Whichever you choose, our advice is to take a morning boat out and a return that lands in Bali well before dark. Travel guides advise against boarding any boat you have doubts about, whether because of the vessel, overloading or the weather.

What this decision actually sits inside

Notice what happened across all of this. Day trip or overnight turned out to be a question about the rest of the itinerary. A day trip starts and ends in Sanur, so it favors a base on that side of Bali. An overnight uses two travel days. And every version has a boat in it, which has to sit somewhere in the trip that a delay would not hurt.

How the island days, the boat crossings and the flight home fit together is worked through in the complete Bali trip guide.

FAQ

Is one day enough for Nusa Penida?

One day covers one side of the island, west or east. Seeing both without rushing takes two days.

How long is the boat from Sanur to Nusa Penida?

Travel guides give the speedboat crossing as roughly 30 minutes. Check times with the operator.

Can you swim at Kelingking Beach?

We have no official source on conditions and call no Penida beach safe for swimming. Travel guides describe the path down as a clifftop descent of about 400 meters.

Is it worth staying overnight on Nusa Penida?

Yes, if you have ten days or more. It lets you see the viewpoints early and late and cover both sides of the island.

Ubud is an inland town in the hills of central Bali, regarded as the island's center for arts and culture. It has rice terraces, temples, museums and a monkey forest, and no beach. It suits travelers who want culture, walking and cooler air, and it is the natural base for the center and east of the island. The town center is busy, and the quiet people imagine is in the villages around it.

What Ubud is

Ubud is a town in central Bali, at about 200 meters above sea level, which makes it cooler than the coast. Travel guides describe it as the cultural center of Bali and its arts and crafts hub. What looks like one town is made up of fourteen villages, each run by its own village committee, known as a banjar.

Where it is

Ubud lies inland, about 22 miles from the airport to Ubud by road. It is about 14 miles from the coast at Sanur and about 19 miles from Canggu. There is no beach. A day at the sea from Ubud is a drive each way, which is a good reason to treat Ubud and the beach as separate parts of a trip.

Which regency

Ubud is in Gianyar regency, a different local government from the beach resorts of the south, which are mostly in Badung. The practical consequence is small: local tax on restaurant and hotel bills is set by each regency, and Gianyar's rate matches Badung's.

How Ubud is laid out

Central Ubud is built around three main streets: Jalan Raya Ubud, Jalan Monkey Forest and Jalan Hanoman. They meet near the market and the palace, which mark the center of town. The Sacred Monkey Forest lies at the southern end of the street named after it. This core can be covered on foot.

The surrounding villages

The villages around the center each have their own character. Campuhan, Sanggingan and Penestanan lie to the north and west; Nyuh Kuning and Pengosekan to the south; Peliatan to the east. Many of the places described as "Ubud" in a hotel listing are in one of these villages, a walk or a short ride from the center.

Traffic in the center

Central Ubud is walkable, and it is congested. Travel guides describe the center as crowded with visitors and the traffic as very bad. The streets are narrow and were not built for the number of cars and motorbikes that now use them. Staying within walking distance of what you want to do saves a great deal of time.

What there is to see

Ubud's sights divide into those in the town and those a drive away. In town are the market, the palace, the museums and the Sacred Monkey Forest. The Campuhan ridge walk starts on the western edge of the center. Outside town are the cave temple of Goa Gajah to the east and the spring temple of Tirta Empul to the north.

Rice terraces

The Tegallalang rice terraces are about 6 miles northeast of central Ubud. Bali's rice-terrace landscape and its water temples are a UNESCO World Heritage site, built on a cooperative irrigation system called subak that dates back to the 9th century. The listing covers five terrace areas and their temples across the island.

Temples and dress

Temple visits around Ubud follow Bali's rules for visitors, which require modest dress in sacred places and bar tourists from the inner courtyards unless they are there to pray in Balinese traditional dress. Our advice is to carry a sarong and a sash, and to cover shoulders and knees.

The monkeys

The Sacred Monkey Forest is a temple site with a large resident population of macaques. The CDC says dogs infected with rabies are commonly found in Indonesia, and its general advice to travelers there is to keep away from animals. Our advice at the forest is to carry no food, keep bags closed, and see a doctor promptly after any bite or scratch.

Day trips from Ubud

Ubud is the best-placed base on the island for the center and the east. By road it is about 27 miles to the crater rim at Kintamani, about 22 to the Sidemen valley, about 39 to Munduk in the mountains and about 49 to Amed on the northeast coast. We give no drive times, since they vary by hour.

What is far from Ubud

The southern beaches are the weak point. Uluwatu is about 34 miles from Ubud, through the busiest roads on the island. A traveler who wants several beach days and several days of temples and terraces will find it easier to split the stay than to commute between the two.

Who Ubud suits

Ubud suits travelers interested in culture, crafts, food, yoga and walking, and anyone who wants a few days away from the beach. Our view is that it suits couples and solo travelers especially well. It is a weaker fit for a trip that is mainly about swimming in the sea, surfing or nightlife.

How long to stay

Our advice is at least three nights, since a day is lost to arriving and the sights lie in several directions. Two nights give one full day, which is enough for the town and not for the surroundings. Travelers who like the pace often wish they had booked more.

Getting around

Inside the center, walk. For the surrounding sights, hire a car and driver for the day or use a ride app for short hops. A scooter requires a license matching the type of vehicle driven under Indonesian law, which for a motorbike means a motorcycle license.

Practical notes

Ubud is cooler than the coast, at about 200 meters of altitude, and evenings can call for a light layer. The climate figures published for south Bali come from a station at sea level and do not describe Ubud, so we give no rainfall numbers for the town. Pack a rain jacket in the wet months.

Money

Bali's rules for visitors say to change money only at authorized changers, which display a license number and a Bank Indonesia logo with a QR code. The State Department advises using ATMs in secure locations such as major bank branches.

FAQ

Is Ubud worth visiting?

Yes, for culture, rice terraces, temples and walking. It has no beach, so it suits a trip that is not only about the sea.

How far is Ubud from the beach?

About 14 miles by road from Sanur and about 19 from Canggu.

How many days do you need in Ubud?

Our advice is at least three nights, which gives two full days for the town and its surroundings.

Is Ubud walkable?

The center is, around three main streets. The surrounding villages and the sights outside town need a car, a driver or a ride app.

The Bukit is the limestone peninsula at Bali's southern tip, and Uluwatu is its best-known corner, named for the temple that stands on a cliff above the sea. The area is known for surf breaks, white sand beaches below cliffs, and sunsets. It is about 13 miles from the airport, and it suits surfers and travelers who want scenery and space more than a walkable town.

What the Bukit is

The Bukit peninsula hangs below the rest of Bali, joined to it by a narrow neck of land where the airport sits. Travel guides describe it as the rugged southernmost part of the island. Uluwatu is on its southwestern corner, Jimbaran at its neck on the west side, and Nusa Dua on its eastern shore.

How it differs from the rest of the south

The Bukit is limestone, and its coast is cliffs with beaches at the bottom, reached by steps. That geography gives the views the area is known for, and it means that a beach day here usually involves a climb.

The regency

The peninsula is part of Badung regency, like Seminyak and Canggu. The local tax on restaurant food and drink and on hotel stays is 10%, with a service charge added separately where a business chooses to add one.

Uluwatu Temple

Uluwatu Temple is the reason the area's name is known. Travel guides describe it as perched on a cliff about 75 meters above the waves. It is a working temple, and Bali's rules for visitors apply: modest dress is required in sacred places, and tourists may not enter the inner courtyards unless they are there to pray in Balinese traditional dress.

Visiting

The temple grounds along the cliff edge are the part visitors walk through. Our advice is to wear clothing that covers shoulders and knees and to accept the sarong and sash offered at the entrance. Keep sunglasses, phones and food secure if there are monkeys about.

Sunset and the dance

The temple is on the west-facing coast, so sunset is the popular hour. A kecak dance is staged for visitors at the temple in the evening; we have not sourced its times or ticket prices, so check locally on the day.

Beaches and surf

The Bukit's beaches are white sand coves at the foot of cliffs, which sets them apart from the long dark-sand beaches further north. Travel guides name Padang Padang among them. Surf guides list the breaks around Uluwatu and Padang Padang among the west-facing spots that are at their best in the dry season.

When the surf works

Surf guides describe the dry season, from about April to October, as the time when southeast trade winds blow offshore on this coast, with the largest swells arriving from June to August. We rate no break for difficulty. Many of the Bukit's waves break over reef, so our advice to a beginner is to take lessons elsewhere first.

Swimming

Reef, tide and swell decide whether a Bukit beach is swimmable on a given day. We have no official source on conditions at each beach, so we describe none as safe. Ask at your accommodation about the tide before you walk down, since some coves have little sand at high water.

The steps

Most Bukit beaches are reached by long flights of steps down the cliff. That is easy going down and hot work coming back. Travelers with small children, heavy bags or limited mobility should ask how many steps a beach involves before choosing it.

Jimbaran and Nusa Dua

The Bukit has two gentler shores. Jimbaran, on the west side near the airport, is described by travel guides as having a sheltered beach and seafood restaurants on the sand. Nusa Dua, on the east side, is an enclave of high-end resorts with a long beach. Uluwatu is about 8 miles from Jimbaran and about 12 from Nusa Dua.

Getting there and around

Uluwatu is about 13 miles from the airport by road, about 17 from Seminyak and about 23 from Canggu. Ubud is about 34 miles away. The peninsula has few through roads, and the drive in and out passes the airport area. We give no drive times; check a live map for your hour.

Getting around the peninsula

The Bukit is spread out, and little of it is walkable. Beaches, restaurants and viewpoints are a drive apart. A car and driver for the day, or a ride app where one is available, is the practical way to move. A scooter requires a license matching the type of vehicle driven.

Ride apps here

We have no official source on ride-app coverage in the Bukit, and it is less built-up than Seminyak or Kuta. Our advice is to arrange your ride back before you set out for a remote beach or the temple at sunset, when many people are leaving at once.

Who the Bukit suits

The Bukit suits surfers, couples and anyone who wants cliff views, quiet and a villa with space around it. It is a weaker fit for travelers who want to walk to a choice of restaurants, for families needing calm shallow water, and for anyone planning many day trips to central Bali.

How long to stay

Our advice is two to four nights for most trips: enough for the temple, a few beaches and some unhurried time. As a day trip from Seminyak or Canggu, the Bukit is possible and involves a long return drive in the evening.

Medical care

The State Department says an injured traveler in Indonesia will likely need to go to a major city for appropriate medical care, and that ambulances can take 45 minutes or longer. On a reef-break coast reached by cliff steps, that is worth knowing before you paddle out.

FAQ

Where is Uluwatu?

On the southwestern corner of the Bukit peninsula at Bali's southern tip, about 13 miles by road from the airport.

Is Uluwatu good for beginner surfers?

We rate no individual break. Many Bukit waves break over reef, so our advice to a beginner is to take lessons at a sandy beach first.

Can you swim at Uluwatu's beaches?

It depends on tide, reef and swell on the day. Ask locally before walking down, since conditions vary by cove.

How far is Uluwatu from Seminyak?

About 17 miles by road. Check a live map for the time, which varies with traffic.

Bali's four best-known temples are in four different corners of the island, and each visit is a different kind of outing. Uluwatu is a clifftop temple in the far south, Tanah Lot a sea temple on the southwest coast, Besakih the mother temple on the slopes of Mount Agung, and Lempuyang a mountain temple in the east famous for one photograph. The same dress and access rules apply at all of them.

The rules that apply at every temple

Bali's rules for foreign tourists apply at every temple on the island. They require modest dress in sacred places, and they bar tourists from the inner and middle courtyards of a temple unless they are there to pray in Balinese traditional dress. Climbing on sacred structures and posing indecently at sacred sites are prohibited.

What to wear

Our advice is the same for all four temples: clothing that covers shoulders and knees, with a sarong and sash where the temple asks for them. Carry your own sarong if you would like to avoid renting one. The circular containing these rules also says that a person entering the inner areas to pray must not be menstruating.

Fees and hours

We list no entrance fees or opening hours, because both change and we have no official source for them. Carry small rupiah notes, and ask your driver or accommodation for the current arrangements the day before.

Uluwatu

Uluwatu Temple stands on the southwestern tip of the Bukit peninsula, and travel guides describe it as perched on a cliff about 75 meters above the sea. It is about 13 miles from the airport by road. The visit is a walk along the cliff edge through the temple grounds, with the ocean below.

What the visit involves

Uluwatu is the easiest of the four to fit into a beach holiday, since it lies in the resort south. It faces west, so sunset is the popular hour, and a kecak dance is staged for visitors at the temple in the evening. We have not sourced its times, so check locally.

Getting back

Our advice is to arrange your ride back before you arrive, since sunset is the popular hour, and to keep sunglasses, phones and food secure if there are monkeys about.

Tanah Lot

Tanah Lot is a sea temple built on a rock just offshore, on the southwest coast. Travel guides describe it as one of Bali's important directional temples, attributed to the 15th-century priest Nirartha. It is about 7 miles up the coast from Canggu by road, which makes it the closest of the four to the west-coast resorts.

What the visit involves

Visitors see Tanah Lot from the shore and the surrounding paths. Travel guides describe the area as very busy, especially in the late afternoon before sunset, with an approach lined by souvenir shops. Under Bali's rules the inner temple is for worshippers, so the visit is to the setting, not the interior.

When to go

Sunset is when the crowds come. Our advice for a calmer visit is to go in the morning, when the light is on the temple instead of behind it. Ask locally about the tide if you hope to walk out toward the rock.

Besakih

Pura Besakih lies on the slopes of Mount Agung in East Bali, and Balinese Hindus regard it as their mother temple. Travel guides describe a complex of more than twenty separate temples spread over about three kilometers. It is about 27 miles from Ubud by road, and far from the southern resorts.

What the visit involves

Besakih is a large site on a mountainside, with stairways and terraces. Allow time to walk it, and expect cooler air and cloud. A ceremony may close parts of the complex to visitors, so ask at the entrance what is open.

Guides and touts

Travel guides mention souvenir sellers in the visitor area. We have no official source on the guiding arrangements at Besakih, so we describe none. Our advice is to ask at the ticket office what your ticket includes before accepting any offer of services on the way in.

Lempuyang

Pura Lempuyang is a temple high in the mountains of Karangasem, in the far east. It is known around the world for one image: a split gate framing Mount Agung, with what looks like a reflection in still water. Lempuyang is about 45 miles from Ubud by road and about 9 from Amed.

The photograph

Travel writers report two things a visitor should know before making the journey. The reflection in the famous picture is made by a photographer holding a mirror under the phone; there is no pool of water at the gate. And the photograph is taken by numbered turn, with a wait that can run to hours.

Is it worth the drive?

Our view is that Lempuyang is worth visiting for travelers already staying in East Bali, around Amed or Sidemen, and hard to justify as a day trip from the south for a single picture. Mount Agung is visible only when the cloud allows, and no one can promise that.

Choosing among them

The four temples suit different trips because of where they are. A traveler based in the south can see Uluwatu and Tanah Lot easily, though not together in one sunset. A traveler based in Ubud or the east is better placed for Besakih and Lempuyang. Few trips need all four.

By base

These are our own suggestions.

  • Staying in the Bukit or Seminyak: Uluwatu.
  • Staying in Canggu: Tanah Lot.
  • Staying in Ubud or Sidemen: Besakih.
  • Staying in Amed: Lempuyang.

Other temples worth knowing

Smaller sites near Ubud can be more rewarding than a long drive to a famous one. Travel guides describe Tirta Empul as a 10th-century spring temple used for ritual purification, Goa Gajah as an 11th-century cave with a carved demon's mouth at its entrance, and Gunung Kawi as an 11th-century site reached by climbing down 371 steps.

Ceremony days

Festival days bring worshippers to the temples. Galungan, which comes every 210 days, falls on January 13 and August 11 in 2027. A visit on such a day is a privilege to watch and calls for extra care about dress, distance and photographs.

FAQ

Which temple in Bali should I visit?

Choose by where you are staying: Uluwatu from the south, Tanah Lot from Canggu, Besakih from Ubud or Sidemen, Lempuyang from Amed.

Can tourists go inside Bali's temples?

Bali's rules bar tourists from the inner and middle courtyards unless they are there to pray in Balinese traditional dress.

Is the water at the Gates of Heaven real?

No. Travel writers report that the reflection is made with a mirror held under the phone by a photographer.

What should I wear to a temple in Bali?

Clothing that covers shoulders and knees, with a sarong and sash where the temple asks for them.

Bali's waterfalls are spread across the island, and almost all of them sit at the bottom of a valley, which means steps down and steps back up. The easiest to reach are near Ubud; the most dramatic are in the north. Each charges its own entrance fee, which we do not list because fees change. Choose waterfalls by where you are staying, not by a ranking.

Where the waterfalls are

Bali's waterfalls fall into three groups by location: those around Ubud in the center, those in the central highlands, and those in the north. The group you can reach depends on your base. Ubud is about 22 miles from the airport and is the best starting point for the first group and a reasonable one for the second.

Around Ubud

Travel guides name four waterfalls in the Ubud area. Tegenungan is about 30 meters high and described as easy to reach. Tibumana, east of Ubud, is a short walk from its parking area. Tukad Cepung is partly hidden in a cave-like canyon and known for light beams. Kanto Lampo involves wading through water for photographs.

The central highlands

Nungnung lies in a jungle ravine north of Denpasar and is reached by about 500 stone steps, according to travel guides. Further up, in the hills near the mountain lakes, are the Banyumala twin falls near Wanagiri and Munduk Waterfall, which guides call perhaps the most impressive accessible falls on the island.

The north

The north has Gitgit, described by travel guides as easy to reach, and Sekumpul, a group of several falls side by side in a jungle valley. These are a long drive from the south: Munduk is about 51 miles from the airport and Lovina about 62. They belong to a stay in the north, not a day trip from Seminyak.

The stairs

Stairs are the common feature of Bali's waterfalls. A waterfall is where a river drops into a gorge, and the parking area is at the top. The walk down is easy and the climb back is hot work in humid air. Nungnung's roughly 500 steps are the best-known example, and it is far from the only one.

Who should think twice

Travelers with knee problems, heart conditions, small children or limited mobility should ask how many steps a waterfall involves before setting out. Tegenungan is described as easy to reach, and Tibumana as a short walk, which makes them the candidates for anyone who wants less climbing.

What to wear

Our advice is sandals or shoes with grip that can get wet, since steps and rocks near a waterfall are slippery. Bring swimwear under your clothes if you plan to get in, a towel, and a dry bag for your phone. Dress modestly on the way through villages, as Bali's rules for visitors ask.

Fees and what they cover

Each waterfall is run locally and charges its own entrance fee, paid at a booth near the parking area. We list no amounts, because fees change and we have no official source. Carry small rupiah notes. Parking and, at some sites, a local guide may be charged separately; ask at the booth what the ticket includes.

Guides

Some waterfalls, particularly the larger ones in the north, are visited with a local guide. We have no official source on where a guide is mandatory, so we state no rule. Ask at the ticket booth, and agree the price before you start walking.

Swimming and safety

Swimming is the reason many people visit a waterfall, and conditions vary by site and by day. We have no official source on water safety at any of them and call none safe. Heavy rain upstream can raise a river quickly. Our advice is to stay out of the water after heavy rain and to follow what local staff tell you.

The wet season

Waterfalls are at their fullest in the wet season, from about November to March, when south Bali's climate record shows 9 to 14 inches of rain a month. That is also when paths are muddiest and water is brownest. The dry season gives clearer pools and easier paths, with less volume.

Water quality

The CDC advises travelers in Indonesia to avoid swimming or wading in water that may be contaminated after flooding. Keep your mouth closed in the water, cover any cuts, and wash afterward. This matters most after rain.

Planning a waterfall day

A waterfall day in Bali works when the falls lie in one direction. Travel guides suggest a route through the Ubud group in a single day. We give no drive times. Our advice is two or three waterfalls, since each one involves a walk down, time at the water and a climb back.

Go early

Our advice is to start early. The best-known waterfalls near Ubud draw many visitors, and the first hours of the day are the quietest and the coolest for the climb back. A driver booked for the day can plan the order to suit.

Combine with what is nearby

A waterfall pairs naturally with something else in the same direction: rice terraces north of Ubud, the mountain lakes near Munduk, or a temple. That makes better use of a driver's day than three waterfalls in a row.

Which waterfall for which traveler

The right waterfall depends on your base and your legs. These are our own suggestions: Tegenungan or Tibumana for an easy visit from Ubud; Tukad Cepung for photographers; Nungnung for those who do not mind the steps; Munduk and Banyumala for a stay in the highlands; Sekumpul for a stay in the north.

Getting there

A car with a driver is the practical way to reach waterfalls, which lie off main roads. A scooter on steep, wet lanes is harder riding than in town, and requires a license matching the type of vehicle driven.

FAQ

What is the easiest waterfall to visit in Bali?

Travel guides describe Tegenungan, near Ubud, as easy to reach, and Tibumana as a short walk from its parking area.

How many steps is Nungnung waterfall?

About 500 stone steps, according to travel guides.

Do Bali waterfalls charge an entrance fee?

Yes, each charges its own fee at a booth near the parking area. We list no amounts because they change.

Can you swim at Bali's waterfalls?

At some. We have no official source on water safety, so ask local staff, and stay out after heavy rain.

One week in Bali is enough for two areas done properly: Ubud for culture and rice terraces, and one beach base in the south. A realistic first-timer route is three nights in Ubud and four by the sea, or the reverse. Seven nights do not stretch to the north, the east and an island as well, and the best one-week trips are the ones that accept that.

What a week can hold

A week in Bali, coming from the United States, is shorter than it looks. The journey has at least one connection and crosses 12 or more time zones, so the first day or two are spent adjusting. The CDC advises allowing at least two days before anything important. Plan five good days and treat the rest as recovery and travel.

Two bases, not four

Bali's beach areas and its cultural center are about 20 miles apart by road, and the drive between them is slow. Our view is that two bases fit a week comfortably and three do not, since each move costs half a day. One coast base and Ubud cover what most first-time visitors come for.

A realistic one-week route

The one-week route below gives a first-time visitor the two sides of Bali with one hotel change. It is a suggestion to adapt, with no drive times and no prices, since both vary. It assumes seven nights on the island and a morning or midday arrival.

  • Day 1: arrive, transfer to Ubud, rest.
  • Day 2: central Ubud on foot; an early night.
  • Day 3: rice terraces and temples north of Ubud with a driver.
  • Day 4: transfer to the coast, with a stop on the way.
  • Days 5 and 6: beach days, with one outing.
  • Day 7: a free day near your hotel.
  • Day 8: depart.

Days 1 to 3: Ubud

Ubud is about 22 miles from the airport to Ubud by road. Spend the first full day on foot in the center: the market, the palace and the Sacred Monkey Forest. On the second, hire a driver for the Tegallalang rice terraces, about 6 miles north, and a temple such as Tirta Empul.

Day 4: the transfer

The move from Ubud to the coast takes part of a day. A driver hired for the transfer can stop on the way, which turns a moving day into a sightseeing one. Agree the stops and the price in writing beforehand, and arrive at the beach in time for the sunset.

Days 5 to 7: the coast

Which coast base depends on what you want. Seminyak suits dining and beach walks, Canggu surfing, the Bukit peninsula cliffs and quiet, and Sanur a calm stay with children. Give these days to the sea, with one outing: Uluwatu Temple from a southern base, or Tanah Lot from Canggu.

Ubud first or beach first?

The order of the two bases is a real choice. Starting in Ubud puts the sightseeing early, while jet lag has you awake at dawn, and ends the trip with rest by the sea, close to the airport. Starting at the beach gives an easy landing after the flight and ends the trip inland, about 22 miles from the terminal.

Our preference

Our view is that Ubud first works better for most first-time visitors. Early mornings suit temples and rice terraces, and the last night falls near the airport. A traveler who arrives late at night may prefer the reverse, to avoid a drive inland in the dark after a long journey.

What to leave out

A one-week trip is defined by what it omits. The north coast and Munduk are about 51 miles or more from the airport. Amed, in the east, is about 61. The Nusa islands need boat crossings that depend on the sea. Each of these deserves its own nights, and a week cannot spare them.

The Mount Batur question

The sunrise trek on Mount Batur is the one long outing that fits a week, because Kintamani is about 27 miles from Ubud. It starts in the middle of the night. Do it on your second or third Ubud morning, never on the first, and keep the rest of that day free.

The island day-trip question

A day trip to Nusa Penida from the south is possible in a week, at the cost of a full day and two boat crossings. Our advice is to choose between that and a rest day, and to place it mid-trip. A boat the day before a long-haul flight is a risk with nothing to gain.

Practical points for a week

A few rules bear on any one-week plan. An American needs a tourist visa, at IDR 500,000, and pays Bali's tourist levy of IDR 150,000 per person. The arrival card can only be filled in during the 72 hours before landing.

Check the calendar

Check your week against Nyepi, the day of silence, which in 2027 falls on Monday, March 8, 2027. Press reports of the 2026 arrangements describe regular flights halting for 24 hours. A day lost that way is a seventh of a one-week trip.

Getting around

Use a driver for the day trips and the transfer, and ride apps for short hops in the south. A scooter requires a license that covers motorcycles under Indonesian law, which most Americans do not hold.

What this decision actually sits inside

Notice what happened across all of this. The route was simple, and almost every line of it depended on something outside the route: the hour your flight lands, the month you travel, whether your coast base suits the season, and how far the last night is from the airport. A day-by-day plan is the visible part. The choices underneath it are what make it work or not.

How to fit those choices to your own dates and flights is worked through in the complete Bali trip guide.

FAQ

Is one week enough for Bali?

Yes, for two areas: Ubud and one beach base. It is not enough to add the north, the east and an island as well.

How should I split a week in Bali?

Our suggestion is three nights in Ubud and four on the coast, with one hotel change.

Should I go to Ubud first or the beach first?

Our view is Ubud first for most visitors, so the last night is near the airport. Late-night arrivals may prefer the beach first.

Can I visit Nusa Penida on a one-week trip?

As a day trip from the south, yes, at the cost of a full day. Place it mid-trip, not the day before your flight.

Two weeks in Bali is enough to leave the south behind for part of the trip. With fourteen nights, a traveler can pair Ubud and a beach base with two of the quieter regions: the central highlands around Munduk, East Bali at Sidemen or Amed, or the Nusa islands. A sensible shape is four bases of three to four nights, moving in one direction around the island.

What two weeks makes possible

Fourteen nights change the arithmetic of a Bali trip. A week covers two areas and ten days three. Two weeks cover four, which is enough to include regions that are too far from the airport for a short stay: Munduk is about 51 miles away by road, and Amed about 61.

The rule of three nights

Our working rule is at least three nights per base, which gives two full days in each. Fourteen nights divided that way gives four bases. A fifth is possible and makes the trip feel like a relay. Our view is that four well-chosen bases beat six hurried ones.

A two-week route

The two-week route below makes a loop through the center, the highlands and the east before finishing on the coast. It is a suggestion to adapt, with no prices and no drive times. Each move is a half-day drive with a driver, and the distances between bases are short in miles.

  • Nights 1 to 4: Ubud.
  • Nights 5 to 7: Munduk and the central highlands.
  • Nights 8 to 10: East Bali, at Sidemen or Amed.
  • Nights 11 to 14: a beach base in the south.

Nights 1 to 4: Ubud

Ubud opens the trip, about 22 miles from the airport. Four nights allow for jet lag, a day on foot in the center, a day of rice terraces and temples, and a sunrise trek on Mount Batur for those who want it, since Kintamani is about 27 miles away.

Nights 5 to 7: Munduk

Munduk is about 39 miles from Ubud by road, and the drive passes the mountain lakes and the temple of Ulun Danu Bratan. Travel guides describe the area as known for waterfalls, coffee and clove plantations and walking, at more than 700 meters of altitude. Pack a sweater.

Nights 8 to 10: the east

From the highlands the route turns east. This is the longest transfer of the trip, about 93 miles to Amed, and it deserves an early start. Sidemen, a valley of rice terraces under Mount Agung, is the alternative for travelers who prefer walking to snorkeling.

Nights 11 to 14: the coast

The trip ends by the sea, close to the airport. From Amed it is about 51 miles to Sanur. Four nights here are for rest, a beach and a last temple visit, with no long drives and no boats before the flight home.

Swapping in an island leg

The Nusa islands can replace either the highlands or the east in this route. Boats leave from Sanur, and travel guides give the crossing as roughly 30 to 45 minutes. An island leg fits best between Ubud and the final coast base, where a delayed boat costs a beach day and nothing more.

Which to swap out

These are our own suggestions. Keep the highlands and swap the east for the islands if you want mountains and sea. Keep the east and swap the highlands for the islands if diving and snorkeling are the point of the trip. Doing all three is possible and leaves little time anywhere.

Why the route runs one way

The order of this route follows the map. Ubud, Munduk, the east and the south form a rough circle, so each drive covers new ground and none doubles back through the busy south. A route that zigzags, from Ubud to Uluwatu and back north to Munduk, spends days on the road.

Transfers as sightseeing

Each transfer is a chance to see what lies between bases. A driver hired for the day can stop at a temple, a waterfall or a viewpoint. Agree the stops and the price in writing beforehand. This is how a two-week trip sees the island without separate day trips.

Start inland, end at the sea

Beginning in Ubud and ending on the coast has two advantages. The early waking of jet lag is put to use among temples and terraces, and the last night falls close to the airport. Reversing the route is workable for travelers who want the beach first.

What two weeks still cannot do

Two weeks are generous and still finite. The far west of the island, with its national park, is a long drive from everything else. The Gili Islands and Lombok need two travel days of their own. Our advice is to leave both for another trip unless one of them is the reason you are coming.

Leave a spare day

A fourteen-night plan with every day assigned is fragile. Rain, a stomach bug or a road closed for a ceremony will take a day from somewhere. Our advice is to leave one day unplanned in the second half, where it can absorb whatever happens.

Practical points for a longer stay

Two weeks are inside the 30 days the tourist visa allows, so no extension is needed. The visa costs IDR 500,000. Check the trip against the calendar: Nyepi falls on Monday, March 8, 2027, and Galungan on January 13 and August 11 that year.

Season

Season shapes this route more than a shorter one, since it visits mountains and two coasts. South Bali's climate record shows about 1 inch of rain in July and about 14 in January. The mountains have their own weather, and the east-facing and west-facing coasts trade places for surf between the seasons.

Medical care and cash

The State Department says adequate medical care may be harder to find in rural areas of Indonesia. Carry the medicine you rely on and enough cash for the quieter regions. How the bases, the transfers and the spare day are ordered for your dates is set out in the complete Bali trip guide.

FAQ

Is two weeks too long for Bali?

No. Fourteen nights allow four bases, including quieter regions such as Munduk and East Bali that a shorter trip cannot reach.

How many places should I stay in two weeks in Bali?

Our suggestion is four bases of three to four nights each.

What is a good two-week Bali route?

Ubud, then Munduk in the highlands, then East Bali at Sidemen or Amed, finishing at a beach base in the south.

Do I need a visa extension for two weeks in Bali?

No. The tourist visa allows a stay of 30 days.
